course.title: Chinese (Pinyin), Start to Fluent
course.subtitle: Mandarin Chinese from absolute beginner through everyday fluency — every lesson shown in pinyin only, so you can start speaking immediately without first learning to read Hanzi characters
course.heroLedeSuffix: Real sentences from lesson one, shown entirely in pinyin — audio is real native-quality Mandarin pronunciation, so your ear learns the real language while your eyes read Latin script.

a1-shi-tobe.title: The Verb 'To Be' (shì)
a1-shi-tobe.explanation: Chinese verbs never conjugate for person or number — shì ('to be') stays exactly the same whether the subject is I, you, he, or they. To negate, place bù directly before it: bú shì ('is not'). There is no equivalent of English am/is/are — just one unchanging word.
a1-shi-tobe.fact: shì is only used to link two nouns (X is Y). To describe a quality with an adjective (e.g. 'I am tall'), Chinese normally drops shì entirely and uses the adjective directly as the predicate: wǒ hěn gāo ('I am very tall') — no shì at all. Inserting shì there is one of the most common mistakes beginners make.

dialogue.native: Shì, wǒ shì xuéshēng. Nǐ ne?
dialogue.en: Yes, I am a student. And you?

dialogue.native: Wǒ bú shì xuéshēng, wǒ shì lǎoshī.
dialogue.en: I'm not a student, I'm a teacher.

a1-negation.title: Negation: bù vs méi
a1-negation.explanation: bù negates almost everything — verbs, adjectives, and future or habitual actions: wǒ bú qù ('I'm not going'), wǒ bù gāo ('I'm not tall'). méi, often as méiyǒu, negates possession ('don't have') and completed past actions: wǒ méiyǒu qián ('I don't have money'), wǒ méi chī zǎofàn ('I didn't eat breakfast'). Crucially, méi is never used with shì — 'is not' is always bú shì, never méi shì.
a1-negation.fact: bù changes tone before another fourth-tone syllable — it becomes second tone (bú) instead of fourth (bù), e.g. 'is not' is pronounced bú shì, not bù shì, even though the underlying word never changes, only the spoken tone. This is why you'll see both bù and bú written in these lessons.

dialogue.native: Méi guānxi, wǒmen míngtiān zài shuō.
dialogue.en: It's okay, we'll talk again tomorrow.

a1-questions.title: Yes/No Questions with ma
a1-questions.explanation: To turn any statement into a yes/no question, simply add the particle ma to the very end — no word order change, no auxiliary verb needed: nǐ shì xuéshēng ('You are a student') → nǐ shì xuéshēng ma? ('Are you a student?'). This is dramatically simpler than English question formation.
a1-questions.fact: ma can never be combined with a question word like shénme ('what') or shéi ('who') in the same sentence — a sentence already containing a question word is already a question, and adding ma on top is a common beginner error that native speakers immediately notice sounds wrong.

dialogue.native: Zhè shì nǐ de bēizi ma?
Bú shì, nà shì tā de.

a1-measure-words.title: Measure Words (liàngcí)
a1-measure-words.explanation: Unlike English, Chinese requires a measure word between a number and almost every noun — you cannot say 'one book' as yī shū, you must say yì běn shū ('one [volume] book'). Different measure words go with different categories of noun: gè is the general, all-purpose measure word usable for most nouns when unsure; běn is for bound printed things like books; zhāng is for flat objects like paper or tickets; zhī is for many animals.
a1-measure-words.fact: gè alone can safely substitute for almost any specific measure word in casual speech and will still be understood — a genuinely useful shortcut for beginners, even though native speakers use the more precise word when they know it.

dialogue.native: Wǒ yào shí gè jiǎozi hé yì bēi chá.
dialogue.en: I'd like ten dumplings and a cup of tea.
